{{Short description|Topological space arising from a usual graph}}
In [[topology]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a '''graph''' is a [[topological space]] which arises from a usual [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] <math>G = (E, V)</math> by replacing vertices by points and each edge <math>e = xy \in E</math> by a copy of the [[unit interval]] <math>I = [0,1]</math>, where <math>0</math> is identified with the point associated to <math>x</math> and <math>1</math> with the point associated to <math>y</math>. That is, as topological spaces, graphs are exactly the [[simplicial complex|simplicial 1-complex]]es and also exactly the one-dimensional [[CW complex]]es.<ref name="hatcher" />

Thus, in particular, it bears the [[quotient topology]] of the [[Set (mathematics)|set]]
:<math>X_0 \sqcup \bigsqcup_{e \in E} I_e</math>
under the quotient map used for gluing. Here <math>X_0</math> is the 0-skeleton (consisting of one point for each vertex <math>x \in V</math>), <math>I_e</math> are the [[interval (mathematics)|closed intervals]] glued to it, one for each edge <math>e \in E</math>, and <math>\sqcup</math> is the [[disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union]].<ref name="hatcher" />

The [[topological space|topology]] on this space is called the '''graph topology'''.

== Subgraphs and trees ==

A '''subgraph''' of a graph <math>X</math> is a [[subspace topology|subspace]] <math>Y \subseteq X</math> which is also a graph and whose nodes are all contained in the 0-skeleton of <math>X</math>. <math>Y</math> is a subgraph [[if and only if]] it consists of vertices and edges from <math>X</math> and is closed.<ref name="hatcher" />

A subgraph <math>T \subseteq X</math> is called a '''tree''' if it is [[Contractible space|contractible]] as a topological space.<ref name="hatcher" /> This can be shown equivalent to the usual definition of a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] in [[graph theory]], namely a [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] graph without [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycles]].

== Properties ==

* The associated topological space of a graph is [[connected space|connected]] (with respect to the graph topology) if and only if the original graph is [[connectivity (graph theory)|connected]].
* Every connected graph <math>X</math> contains at least one [[maximal element|maximal]] tree <math>T \subseteq X</math>, that is, a tree that is maximal with respect to the order induced by set inclusion on the subgraphs of <math>X</math> which are trees.<ref name="hatcher" />
* If <math>X</math> is a graph and <math>T \subseteq X</math> a maximal tree, then the [[fundamental group]] <math>\pi_1(X)</math> equals the [[free group]] generated by elements <math>(f_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}</math>, where the <math>\{f_\alpha\}</math> correspond [[bijective]]ly to the edges of <math>X \setminus T</math>; in fact, <math>X\setminus T</math> is [[homotopy equivalence|homotopy equivalent]] to a [[wedge sum]] of [[circle]]s.<ref name="hatcher" />
* Forming the topological space associated to a graph as above amounts to a [[functor]] from the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of graphs to the [[category of topological spaces]].
* Every [[covering space]] projecting to a graph is also a graph.<ref name="hatcher" />
